name: Voonik
epitaph: Tried on five business models. None fit.
oneLiner: A women's fashion app that started as a personal stylist on your phone, then became a marketplace, a premium store and a private label.
causeOfDeath: It spent big on ads, hiring and acquisitions before the core business worked, then ran out of investor money and pivoted until nothing was left to sell.
moneyNote: About $27M raised from 2013 to 2016, as reported by Inc42. No valuation or merger price was ever disclosed. Rupee figures are as filed; Inc42 converted FY16 at about ₹65 per dollar.
inOneMinute: Voonik began as a clever **'personal stylist' app** for Indian women and grew to 10 million registered users.
In FY16 it **lost ₹84 crore on ₹16 crore of revenue**, spending heavily on ads, hiring and six small acquisitions.
After about **five pivots**, it was split up in 2020: its tech went to Bangladesh's ShopUp, its shop to a kidswear brand.
killerLine: A pivot should be a step, not a habit. **Fix one business before you buy, launch or become another.**

chapters.title: The idea: a stylist in every phone
chapters.body: In 2013, Sujayath Ali and Navaneetha Krishnan started Voonik in Bengaluru as a **personal shopping app for women**. You told it about your body type, lifestyle and budget, and it suggested clothes from many online stores. You swiped yes or no on items, like a dating app for kurtas, and every swipe taught it your taste. Ali said the styling engine had "more than 10,000 rules". Voonik held no stock and did no deliveries. It sent orders to partner stores like Jabong and took about **15% commission**. By June 2015 it had around a million downloads and about 2,500 purchases a day, and Sequoia led a $5 million investment. It was a smart, low-cost model with a real customer problem behind it.

chapters.title: The rise: buying, launching, spending
chapters.body: Then Voonik sped up in every direction at once. From August 2015 it acqui-hired (bought mainly to get the team) a virtual dressing-room startup, a men's shopping app, a designer marketplace, an online silk saree store and even **a salon-booking app**, which simply stopped running. In June 2016 it raised **$20 million** led by Sequoia and Beenos and launched Vilara, a premium store for designers and boutiques. In September it bought Dekkoh, a styling app. It claimed 10 million registered users and 15 lakh products. But money was pouring out on hiring, marketing and advertising. In FY16 it **lost ₹84 crore on revenue of only ₹16 crore**. That is about ₹5 lost for every ₹1 earned.

chapters.title: The cracks: the money stops
chapters.body: After the June 2016 round, Voonik **could not raise fresh funding**. The market had turned. Online fashion was crowded with Myntra, Jabong, Amazon and Limeroad, and Aditya Birla had just shut its own fashion site, abof. In November 2017 reports said Voonik asked many employees to defer salaries. Ali denied the specific claim, but told ET that some staff were asked to "self-select" into a final push to profit, "which includes deference of salary if required". In January 2018 he said on Twitter that Voonik had reached **monthly EBITDA profit** (profit before interest, tax and some accounting costs). He said it came from "change in fundamentals of the business", not from cutting marketing.

chapters.title: The fall: split into pieces
chapters.body: The profit did not lead to growth. Voonik kept changing shape, about five times in all. In May 2019 it moved to selling only its own private-label clothes. By FY19, revenue had shrunk to **₹21 crore**, with a ₹17 crore loss. In February 2020 Voonik merged its business tools and technology into **ShopUp**, a Bangladesh startup that helps small sellers run shops on Facebook. Both founders joined ShopUp as co-founders. Voonik's consumer shop in India went to Schoolay, a kidswear maker run by a former Voonik executive. Media called it a distress sale, saying Voonik could not find buyers in India. Its FY20 accounts showed a ₹28.9 crore profit, but by then Voonik was no longer an independent company.

charts.title: Revenue vs net result
charts.takeaway: Revenue jumped once money was spent on growth (FY17 is the company's own claim), then collapsed when the spending stopped.

mistakes.title: Spending like a giant before the model worked
mistakes.explain: In FY16, Voonik **lost ₹84 crore while earning ₹16 crore**. Inc42 said the burn "skyrocketed" from hiring, marketing and ads. That only works if the next funding round is certain. It was not: after June 2016, Voonik could not raise again, and every later decision was made under pressure.

mistakes.title: Six acquisitions in about a year
mistakes.explain: A dressing-room tool, a men's app, a designer marketplace, a silk store, a styling app and **a salon-booking app**. Each one needed attention and money. For a young startup, every acquisition is a new product to run. Most of these teams were absorbed and their products closed, as Styl's was right away.

mistakes.title: Pivoting again and again
mistakes.explain: Voonik went from stylist app to marketplace, premium store, styling chat, private label and B2B tools: **about five pivots**. Each change reset what customers knew about the brand and what the team was good at. Changing direction is fine once or twice. Doing it constantly means you never learn whether any one model could work.

mistakes.title: Fighting where giants were strongest
mistakes.explain: Its first model sent shoppers to big stores like Jabong for a 15% cut. That made Voonik **dependent on the very companies it competed with**. Myntra, Jabong and Amazon could outspend it on ads and discounts. Its real edge, personal styling, was never made big enough to stand alone.

warningSigns: Are we losing more than ₹2 for every ₹1 of revenue, with no clear date when that flips?
Is our plan to survive based on a funding round that has not been signed yet?
Have we bought or launched a product this year that has nothing to do with our main customer?
Would different people on our team describe what our business is in different ways?
Do our biggest partners also compete with us for the same customer?
Have we changed our business model more than twice in two years?

lessons.title: Earn the right to spend
lessons.detail: Before you spend heavily on ads, prove that a customer who comes once comes back on their own. If repeat buying is weak, more ads just buy more one-time visitors.

lessons.title: Say no to shiny acquisitions
lessons.detail: Buying a small team can feel like progress. But each one brings new products, new people and new problems. Only buy what directly makes your main product better for your main customer.

lessons.title: Set a rule for pivots
lessons.detail: Before you pivot, write down what you tried, how long you gave it, and the number that proved it failed. If you can't name that number, you may be quitting too early, or running away from a hard problem.

lessons.title: Grow your real edge
lessons.detail: Voonik's styling engine was what made it different. Ask: is our special thing getting more money and attention every month, or less? If less, you are slowly turning into a copy of your rivals.

lessons.title: Plan for 'no new money'
lessons.detail: Make a version of your plan that assumes no investor will give you money for 18 months. If the company dies in that version, cut costs now, while you still have choices, not after the bank balance forces you.

quote.text: Voonik is joining hands with ShopUp, a rocketship startup from Bangladesh.
quote.who: Sujayath Ali, co-founder and CEO of Voonik
quote.context: Announcing on Twitter in February 2020 that Voonik's business and team would merge into ShopUp.

afterlife.text: Voonik's founders became co-founders of ShopUp in Dhaka, which helps small Bangladeshi sellers run Facebook shops and get loans. The Voonik platform was reused for ShopUp's business tools. In October 2020 ShopUp raised $22.5 million led by Sequoia Capital India and Flourish Ventures. It is a real comeback story: the product and the people found a second life, even if the Voonik brand did not.
